candidates.lead: Greater Manchester's School Streets scheme encourages more children to walk, cycle or scoot to school
candidates.evidence_text: Banning cars near schools at rush hour 'would make big difference' - BBC News Image caption, The Dean Trust academy in Ardwick is one of the schools wanting to join the School Streets scheme By Davinia Ramos North West Published 1 hour ago A head teacher has said he would support his school joining a scheme designed to ban most cars from parking around it during peak times. Steven Worthington, who runs the Dean Trust Ardwick in east Manchester, said there had been "a number of incidents" and "our young people are subjected to bad traffic pollution". He told the BBC that "traffic is very congested during school drop-off and pick-up times... we're keen to address this''. Greater Manchester's School Streets initiative - which also encourages children to walk, cycle or scoot - was launched five years ago and now covers 51 schools and more than 20,000 pupils. By 2030, Transport for Greater Manchester wants 70% of primary school pupils to walk, wheel, scoot or cycle to and from school. Image caption, The School Streets programme is designed to persuade more children to walk to and from school Roads surrounding the Dean Trust Academy are chaotic at peak times, with motorists often parking on double yellow lines or leaving their engines running while waiting for their children to finish school. One parent Lisa Moores said: "It's really busy - loads of children are trying to cross the road at the same time and cars are trying to navigate round them, I've had a few run-ins with people not giving way. "Having restrictions down here would make a big difference during certain times of day." Worthington said he would like to implement the School Streets programme. Under it, traffic is restricted at drop-off and pick-up times on certain roads surrounding schools. Anyone who breaches the restrictions and is filmed by ANPR cameras gets a written warning. Repeat offenders are fined £70. 'Giving parents a choice' One of the schools that has signed up to the scheme is Acacias Community Primary School in Burnage, south Manchester. During two periods - from 08:15 to 09:00 and 15:00 to 15:45 - vehicle access around the school is restricted on weekdays. Roads are only open to pedestrians, cyclists, and exempted vehicles such as emergency services, Blue Badge holders and eligible local residents. Greater Manchester's active travel commissioner Dame Sarah Storey said: "This is about giving parents a choice, lots of people don't feel it's safe for their children to walk to school and this scheme encourages them to do so". One parent of a pupil at Acacias said: "I think it's a great idea to walk to school and safer not to drive. "There are too many cars on the road, and this is much better and healthier." candidates.lead: People describe a "horrible smell" and hearing screaming as they were evacuated from the Don Toliver gig
candidates.evidence_text: Manchester's Co-op Live evacuated after 'unknown substance' let off in crowd at concert by US rapper Don Toliver - BBC News To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: Coughing, confusion and boos as Co-op Live concert cancelled By Chris Graham , Stewart Whittingham , North West and Judith Moritz , Special correspondent , Reporting from at Co-Op Live, Manchester Published 23 November 2026 Police are investigating after thousands of people were evacuated from a concert in Manchester following an "unknown substance" being released into the crowd. It happened towards the end of US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live arena at about 22:00 GMT on Sunday, with fans describing a "horrible smell" and people "screaming" and "coughing up blood". One woman was taken to hospital for treatment, while 88 other people were assessed by paramedics for "eye and respiratory symptoms". Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said detectives were trying to establish what the substance was and where it came from and further testing was taking place on items found at the venue. A major incident was declared after reports of people suffering from the effects of an unknown substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas. That major incident status was lifted at about 04:00 GMT. The force said no arrests had yet been made and detectives were investigating "whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident". GMP said 88 people underwent "dry decontamination at the scene" and were accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed. Some 12,000 people were evacuated and one fan told of "distressing scenes" with people "choking" and coughing as they left the venue. Some fans have complained about security and a lack of searches going in to the concert. A group of friends from Scunthorpe was standing in the mosh pit when the substance was released and said they "heard a pop" and "everyone coughing" and running away. Molly, 19, said: "People not breathing, gagging, gasping for air. It was quite traumatic. "People being wheeled out in wheelchairs covered in tinfoil, and no-one in the venue knew what was going on." Kyan, 22, said: "When you breathed it in you tasted something weird. It didn't sit right - constant coughing, it sent a sting into your eyes." The friends were later taken to the Etihad Stadium for the decontamination process. Jack, 21, said some people had "pink liquid" on them and they were taken off to be tested. "We were told to take off our clothes, and put on hazmat suits, slippers and a mask and taken to the Etihad to be observed," he said. Charlie, 20, said he found the process a bit "invasive" and "confusing". The friends said they were still suffering from symptoms, with a headache, chest pains and "really sore throat". 'People were screaming in pain' during Co-op Live evacuation Image caption, Molly, 19, Kyan 22, Charlie, 20, and Jack, 21, say they were taken to the decontamination process Joey Howe was at the gig and recalled the incident happening 30 or 40 minutes in. The 22-year-old told BBC Radio Manchester : "I saw a lot of people streaming out and you go into this panic mode and you see a lot of people running out of the venue. "The lights have come on and he is being rushed off stage. "That horrible smell just hit you." To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Joey Howe says he wondered if it was "part of the show" until the smell hit He said it was like "time stopped in motion" when "there was nothing going on". "We then decided to go out. People were coming through in wheelchairs choking - it was really distressing," Howe said. "We then decided to leave the venue. It was just really distressing scenes and not something you want to see." Howe also claimed security was "poor" and "very relaxed" with "people walking straight in". 'Screaming in pain' Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they had fled the venue. The 23-year-old told the BBC that she went to the exit and saw lads on the bridge which leads into Medlock Square "asking for help" but there were only two stewards outside. She said she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size". Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Concertgoers headed home after the performance was stopped by the incident Malachi Clar

evidence_packet.evidence_text: A row over changes to planning rules has left a Greater Manchester council unable to make planning decisions, including in Angela Rayner's constituency The housing secretary's department has introduced reforms intended to speed up housebuilding by allowing officers to sign off smaller schemes without councillor involvement In Tameside, which has a Labour-led minority administration, opposition councillors have refused to adopt the changes at successive meetings Subsequently, the authority said "no planning decisions or determinations" were currently being made Councillors still have a say on larger developments, which will continue to go before planning committees, but smaller and more technical applications will only be dealt with by planning officers Reform UK is the second largest party in Tameside and its group leader Allan Hopwood has vowed to continue fighting the changes

candidates.evidence_text: A head teacher has said he would support his school joining a scheme designed to ban most cars from parking around it during peak times Steven Worthington, who runs the Dean Trust Ardwick in east Manchester, said there had been "a number of incidents" and "our young people are subjected to bad traffic pollution" He told the BBC that "traffic is very congested during school drop-off and pick-up times... we're keen to address this'' Greater Manchester's School Streets initiative - which also encourages children to walk, cycle or scoot - was launched five years ago and now covers 51 schools and more than 20,000 pupils By 2030, Transport for Greater Manchester wants 70% of primary school pupils to walk, wheel, scoot or cycle to and from school Roads surrounding the Dean Trust Academy are chaotic at peak times, with motorists often parking on double yellow lines or leaving their engines running while waiting for their children to finish school

candidates.evidence_text: A row over changes to planning rules has left a Greater Manchester council unable to make planning decisions, including in Angela Rayner's constituency The housing secretary's department has introduced reforms intended to speed up housebuilding by allowing officers to sign off smaller schemes without councillor involvement In Tameside, which has a Labour-led minority administration, opposition councillors have refused to adopt the changes at successive meetings Subsequently, the authority said "no planning decisions or determinations" were currently being made Councillors still have a say on larger developments, which will continue to go before planning committees, but smaller and more technical applications will only be dealt with by planning officers Reform UK is the second largest party in Tameside and its group leader Allan Hopwood has vowed to continue fighting the changes

candidates.evidence_text: Salford Historic £1.4m Salford church with 4am party licence up for sale - and the extraordinary story of the street around it Built in 1819 in a post-Napoleonic surge of religious fervour - and later rocked by a minister's mysterious scandal - the Gr Add to preferred sources Comments News Neal Keeling Chief reporter 06:23, 24 Nov 2026 An empty Georgian church may be on the brink of salvation. The former Hope United Reformed Church in Chapel Street, Salford , dates from 1819 Close to Manchester city centre and less than 100 yards from Salford Central railway station it ceased to be a regular place of worship several years ago. Grade II listed, it is now up for sale for offers in excess of £1.4m Its roots lie in a surge of "Christian fervour" across the country at the end of the Napoleonic Wars. It sprang from a dearth of places to hear the Gospel in the rapidly industrialising Salford. It survived as a church through name changes, and the resignation of its first leader A dwindling congregation eventually meant a final Sunday Service was held in 2019. In 2023 plans to convert it into a complex of flats, a community centre and commercial use were submitted to the City Council Hope United Reformed Church on Chapel St, Salford, pictured today. It is up for sale for £1.4m. (Image: Manchester Evening News)

Here' Add to preferred sources News Liv Clarke Tourism writer 06:22, 24 Nov 2026 On May 21, 2025 I boarded a flight from Manchester Airport, just like hundreds of other passengers that day. candidates.evidence_text: Bolton Home Office stops using 'inappropriate family home' in Horwich for asylum seekers after backlash The Home Office has said the terraced property will no longer be used for asylum purposes Add to preferred sources Comments News Chris Gee Local de Asylum seekers will no longer be housed in what a MP described as ‘an inappropriate family home’ in Horwich. Described by a local councillor as ‘a horrendous blight’, the terraced property on Brownlow Road was being used by Serco, who manage government-funded housing and support Bolton North MP Phil Brickell said that after he campaigned on behalf of unhappy residents, ‘direct ministerial intervention’ led to the property close to the town centre being deemed unacceptable for housing asylum seekers He said: “These people have now been re-located and the property will no longer be used by the Home Office. I will continue to monitor developments relating to the ongoing use of the property closely and make representations on behalf of constituents where necessary.” The announcement has led to a dispute between Mr Brickell and local councillors in Horwich, who have also been chasing the issue on behalf of neighbours Horwich and Blackrod First (HBFI) leader David Grant said the decision ‘had nothing to do with any Government pressure’ and had come about through tougher new council licensing on HMOs which he and others had been instrumental in introducing

A major incident was declared at 10.25pm last night (November 22), following the release of an unknown substance at around 10pm More than 80 people went on to be assessed by medics, with one person taken to hospital. Greater Manchester Police is yet to confirm the nature of the substance or how it was released inside the venue Gig goers have described how the substance was released in the standing area of the UK's biggest arena. Multiple fans have reported bags not being searched on entrance, and questioned whether security measures at the arena's entrance were tight enough Vic Fearon, 51, attended the gig with her daughter Charlotte, 21. Vic, who was seated close to the stage, said: "We could see the standing areas. They were all really rowd

candidates.evidence_text: Oldham The Oldham road becoming a council cash cow as 4,000 motorists are fined A council spokesperson said: "This funding helps maintain roads, including pothole repairs and road markings, provide and maintain parking facilities, and support environm More than 4,000 fines have been handed out on a single road in Oldham , contributing to the council’s £1million of profit from parking over one year, new data shows In recent months, people in Oldham have complained of parking issues in parts of the borough with some claiming not enough is being done to tackle pavement parking and drivers ignoring double yellow lines. This is despite thousands of fines being given out and action taken in are Now a Freedom of Information request submitted to Oldham council shows action has been taken across parts of the borough. In the financial year between April 2025 and March 2026, 34,957 parking fines were handed out by the local authority An additional 18,042 fines were then handed out between April 2026 and the end of September this year. This brings the total handed over 18 months to 52,999 fines Despite this, a number of fines still remain unpaid with more than 11,000 are outstanding. Only seven were successfully overturned on appeal

candidates.evidence_text: Salford Historic £1.4m Salford church with 4am party licence up for sale - and the extraordinary story of the street around it Built in 1819 in a post-Napoleonic surge of religious fervour - and later rocked by a minister's mysterious scandal - the Gr Add to preferred sources Comments News Neal Keeling Chief reporter 06:23, 24 Nov 2026 An empty Georgian church may be on the brink of salvation. The former Hope United Reformed Church in Chapel Street, Salford , dates from 1819 Close to Manchester city centre and less than 100 yards from Salford Central railway station it ceased to be a regular place of worship several years ago. Grade II listed, it is now up for sale for offers in excess of £1.4m Its roots lie in a surge of "Christian fervour" across the country at the end of the Napoleonic Wars. It sprang from a dearth of places to hear the Gospel in the rapidly industrialising Salford. It survived as a church through name changes, and the resignation of its first leader A dwindling congregation eventually meant a final Sunday Service was held in 2019. In 2023 plans to convert it into a complex of flats, a community centre and commercial use were submitted to the City Council Hope United Reformed Church on Chapel St, Salford, pictured today. It is up for sale for £1.4m. (Image: Manchester Evening News)

A major incident was declared at 10.25pm last night (November 22), following the release of an unknown substance at around 10pm More than 80 people went on to be assessed by medics, with one person taken to hospital. Greater Manchester Police is yet to confirm the nature of the substance or how it was released inside the venue Gig goers have described how the substance was released in the standing area of the UK's biggest arena. Multiple fans have reported bags not being searched on entrance, and questioned whether security measures at the arena's entrance were tight enough Vic Fearon, 51, attended the gig with her daughter Charlotte, 21. While Vic had her bag searched - leading to a bag of Jelly Babies and a bottle of water being confiscated - she says her daughter was only asked what was inside her handbag, before security staff 'took her word for Hours later, the Accrington pair - who have been to Co-op Live several times before - noticed a flare was among the items that other concertgoers had been able to smuggle in. Vic, who was seated close to the stage, said: "We could see the standing areas. They were all really rowd

Described by a local councillor as ‘a horrendous blight’, the terraced property on Brownlow Road was being used by Serco, who manage government-funded housing and support Bolton North MP Phil Brickell said that after he campaigned on behalf of unhappy residents, ‘direct ministerial intervention’ led to the property close to the town centre being deemed unacceptable for housing asylum seekers He said: “These people have now been re-located and the property will no longer be used by the Home Office. candidates.evidence_text: Co-Op Live Over 80 treated at Manchester's Co-op Live after 'tear gas' released in Don Toliver concert A major incident was declared Add to preferred sources Comments News Stephen Topping Senior reporter 12:37, 23 Nov 2026 Ambulances outside Co-op Liv More than 80 people have been assessed by medics after suspected tear gas was released at a Co-op Live concert. Don Toliver's gig came to a halt at around 10pm last night (November 22) after an unknown substance was released Gig goers have described suffering sore eyes, sore throats and headaches following the incident. One fan said she saw a group of young men 'crying and screaming for help' after leaving the UK's largest arena In an update issued this morning (Monday), North West Ambulance Service (NWAS) says more than 80 people were assessed by clinicians following last night's major incident at Co-op Live. It confirmed that decontamination has also taken place as a precaution An NWAS spokesperson said: "At 10.25pm, we declared a major incident following reports of a substance being released inside the arena. We sent several emergency crews to the scene, including our Hazardous Area Response Team, to assess and care for those affected "Our clinicians assessed more than 80 people, some of whom experienced eye and respiratory symptoms. Decontamination was carried out as a precaution, and one patient was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment

A major incident has been declared by police. . . . . . . Add to preferred sources . . Comments . . News . Charlotte Fisher Reporter . . 00:07, 23 Nov 2026 Updated 06:18, 23 Nov 2026 . . . . . . Scene inside Co-op live during Don Toliver gig . . . . Concertgoers at Co-op Live in Manchester were evacuated on Sunday night (November 22), during Don Toliver’s NITROUS show. Emergency services and police attended the scene and a cordon was put in place outside the venue.. Eyewitnesses said the standing area was cleared at around 10pm, shortly after Don Toliver finished performing on the B stage.. Greater Manchester Police said an 'unknown substance' - reported to be tear gas - was released into the crowd towards the end of the concert.. Over 12,000 fans in attendance were evacuated immediately.. A major incident was declared by police, with one fan in hospital.. Over 50 people fell ill and were medically assessed, paramedics said.. A video that captured the moment officials formally stopped the event shows a staff member telling the audience the show was finished and asked people to leave via the nearest exit.. GMP said those showing signs of being affected were being supported by emergency services. Police added that no serious injuries had been reported but one person was in hospital.. Police asked people to stay away from the arena while emergency services managed the evacuation and helped concertgoers get to transport home.. In a statement, Co-op Live said it will work with police to identify what happened and 'appropriate action' to be taken.. Emergency services have also told anyone who was at the gig to seek medical attention if they feel unwell in the next few days.. No arrests have been at this stage, and nor have any serious injuries been reported.. READ THE FULL STORY: LIVE: Co-op Live evacuated and police descend on venue . . Follow men: Facebook . It was initially thought tear gas was released into the crowd, but GMP later said it was an ‘unknown substance’ Videos shared on social media, taken from the floor standing area, revealed attendees had to quickly cover their faces with T-shirts, and began coughing violently before escaping from the substance by heading to the concourse One screamed: “It burns!”. Another shouted "What the f*** was that smell bro? I can't breathe bro. Bro what was that?!" Molly, a 22-year-old fan who made her way from Derbyshire for the gig, had a bird’s eye view of the incident on the balcony. She saw gaps in the crowd opening up ‘40 minutes in’ “All of a sudden everyone was running out, coughing,” she told the Manchester Evening News . “The security and Co-op [Live] staff did not tell us anything and just said it was a break and we were not told we were being evacuated

candidates.evidence_text: Wednesday 14 October 2026 at 10:33am Kirith Entwistle, the Labour MP for Bolton North East, has said she found the current court system "triggering" and had to watch her abuser "stare at her". Credit: UK Parliament A Labour MP has revealed that she is a victim of domestic abuse - Speaking in the Commons on October 13, Kirith Entwistle, who represents Bolton North East, described her experience of the current court system as "triggering", adding that she had to watch her abuser "stare at her" during a recent video hearing Ms Entwistle told her fellow MPs that she believes special measures - where victims are given protection or assistance in court - should be the standard in cases involving domestic abuse Examples of these measures could include screens, the ability to give evidence through a live link, or witnesses being able to be accompanied when giving evidence Measures to protect victims are included in the Courts and Tribunals Bill, which is currently going through Parliament Speaking during a debate on the bill, Ms Entwistle said: "It doesn’t matter how many times somebody tells me that they understand what I’m going through, or they acknowledge what I’ve been through, they really don’t unless they have lived it themselves or know somebody who has."

candidates.lead: The scheme would sit on a sit partly occupied by GRUB.
candidates.evidence_text: The scheme would sit on a sit partly occupied by GRUB. Credit: via Font Comms A little over a year since plans were unveiled, the Guernsey-based investor behind the 509-flat scheme has formally submitted its proposals to Manchester City Council Designed by Jon Matthews Architects, LWP Red Bank’s development features 18- and 43-storey elements on a one-acre site off Red Bank The plot, previously occupied by GRUB, sits within the Victoria North masterplan that FEC is bringing forward in partnership with Manchester City Council. The aim of Victoria North is to regeneration 390 acres of North Manchester into 15,000 homes over the next 15 to 20 years In Red Bank specifically, the plan is for 5,500 homes, many of which would be delivered on land south of LWP Red Bank’s site that has been remediated with £51m of Homes England funding LWP Red Bank’s scheme would feature a mix of one- to three-bed flats and would have a gross development value of between £151m and £166m depending on tenure, according to a viability appraisal carried out by CBRE. No affordable homes are proposed on viability grounds

candidates.summary: There would also be a clubhouse, formed from modified shipping containers

candidates.lead: There would also be a clubhouse, formed from modified shipping containers
candidates.evidence_text: Plans unveiled for four new padel courts at Hale Barns hotel Skip to content News — Sport & Leisure Plans unveiled for four new padel courts at Hale Barns hotel There would also be a clubhouse, formed from modified shipping containers. , and David Prior November 23, 2026 . 10:14 AM 2 min read Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Share via Email Plans have been submitted to build four padel courts at a hotel in Hale Barns – but permission is being sought for just five years. Padel Investments Ltd has applied to Trafford Council to create the courts, a single-storey clubhouse and a retractable canopy at Delta Hotels by Marriott Manchester Airport on Hale Road. The proposed development would occupy a site in the north-east corner of the hotel grounds, close to the M56, which was previously used for outdoor tennis courts and is now used for overflow parking. The four courts would be positioned side by side, with retractable roof coverings allowing play throughout the year. A clubhouse, formed from modified shipping containers, would include an office, seating and a refreshment area. The proposals also include formalising 84 parking spaces for shared use by the hotel and padel facility, including six accessible bays. Access would remain through the hotel's existing entrance. A visual showing how a sitting area close to the courts would look According to the planning documents, the courts would operate between 7am and 9pm, seven days a week, including bank holidays. They would form part of the hotel's existing leisure club facilities, with the applicant stating that they would be available to hotel guests and private individuals, including members of the local community. No prices, membership arrangements or opening date have been confirmed. The unusual five-year permission request relates to the site's location within land safeguarded for the former HS2 route between Crewe and Manchester. Although that section of the high-speed railway was cancelled, the applicant says safeguarding restrictions remain in place. The four courts would be positioned side by side, with retractable roof coverings allowing play throughout the year The planning statement argues that the temporary nature of the development would allow the courts and associated structures to be removed if required for any future rail project. The site is also within the Green Belt, although the applicant argues that the proposals are acceptable under planning policy. An acoustic assessment submitted with the application concludes that noise from the courts would be below existing ambient sound levels at the nearest homes, with traffic from the M56 already dominating the local noise environment. The applicant also proposes LED floodlighting designed to minimise light spill beyond the courts. The courts would be located at Delta Hotels by Marriott Manchester Airport Padel is already available locally at Hale Country Club and Dunham Forest Golf Club, while Trafford Council approved plans for two further courts at Altrincham Golf Club in June. The latest application, reference 120106/FUL/26, was validated on November 20 and is awaiting a decision. Residents can submit comments through Trafford Council's planning portal, with the neighbour consultation period running until December 14. candidates.evidence_text: The proposed parking changes are expected to take effect in summer 2027 Share on WhatsApp Share via Email Trafford councillors have rejected calls to scrap planned parking charges in Timperley and the proposed introduction of evening and Sunday charges across the borough At Wednesday night’s Full Council meeting, a Conservative amendment calling for the proposals to be withdrawn was defeated, while a Labour amendment removing opposition to the extension of parking charges was passed The original Liberal Democrat motion, tabled by Timperley North councillor Jane Brophy, had warned that extending charges to smaller district centres risked damaging businesses already facing significant pressures Labour’s successful amendment removed that commitment, replacing it with a statement that “Parking charges should reflect the different needs and offers in areas across Trafford.” The vote does not, however, mean the proposed charges have been formally approved

candidates.evidence_text: Children and families are set to benefit from improved play areas in Failsworth after Oldham Council secured £270,000 from the Government's Playground Fund The funding forms part of an £18million government programme to create or refurbish playgrounds in England's areas of greatest need over the next two years The government selected Failsworth to receive a share of the fund, with three play areas identified as eligible for investment through the programme for 66 local authorities Funding will be used to improve playground facilities and support community-led design and engagement activities, giving residents the opportunity to help shape the future of these spaces The three eligible sites are Higher Memorial Park which will receive £160,000, Daisy Nook Country Park which will receive £60,000 and Lower Memorial Park which has been allocated £50,000 A larger share will go to Higher Memorial Park because this has received significantly less external investment than the other locations in recent years

candidates.evidence_text: Residents in Saddleworth will have the opportunity to vote on the future of planning in their area when a referendum takes place on Thursday 10 December 2026 The referendum will ask residents whether they want Oldham Council and the Peak District National Park Authority to use the Saddleworth Neighbourhood Plan to help decide planning applications in the area The plan sets out local planning policies for Saddleworth and, if approved, will become part of the area’s statutory Development Plan, helping to guide decisions on future planning applications Residents will be asked the following question “Do you want Oldham Council and the Peak District National Park Authority to use the Neighbourhood Plan for Saddleworth to help it decide planning applications in the neighbourhood area?” To vote, residents must be registered to vote in local government elections and have a qualifying address within the Saddleworth Neighbourhood Area

Each included the immemorial words from Laurence Binyon’s 1914 poem, For the Fallen: “They shall grow not old as we that are left grow old; Age shall not weary them, nor the years condemn; at The Armed Forces community, Members of Parliament, Mayor of Rochdale, Council Leader, Councillor Neil Emmott, councillors, faith leaders, local schools and members of the public also laid their own wreaths and gave respects, following moving readings of The Kohima Epitaph: “When Mayor of Rochdale, Councillor Faisal Rana, said “The turnout across the borough was incredible, as people of all ages gathered at memorials in Heywood, Middleton, Pennines, and Rochdale to pay their respects. On a poignant and moving Remembrance Day, we honoured the fallen, people of all faiths and no faith, from countries all

candidates.evidence_text: Bolton’s providing new forms of support for residents struggling with the cost of living, as presented at Bolton’s Tackling Poverty networking event held at Bolton Albert Halls on November 12 The cost of living is a major concern for many, and it may get tougher during the winter, as such, the event and the targeted support offered to people across Bolton offer some reassurance to those worst affected The support spans a large number of areas including helping access emergency food, heating, and financial assistance The event brings those organisations providing support together so they can better understand what is available across the town and as such can make informed decisions about who to refer people to for the most appropriate help In total there were over 40 organisations attending the event including the public, voluntary, and community sector, and other parters who were highlighting their services all were encouraged to network, share information, and create a more connected and efficient framework The presentations highlighted how Bolton’s Tacking Poverty Strategy can make a real difference, and how the Crisis, and Resilience Fund is being allocated to help groups across the borough

candidates.evidence_text: Experience the raw, unfiltered power of Balkan folklore in a new immersive show from the world’s most famous performance artist Balkan Erotic Epic is a bold new performance work created by the iconic artist Marina Abramović . Regarded as the world’s most influential performance artist, Abramović’s transformative work has reached millions of people – from opening the Pyramid Stage at Glastonbury Festival t A four-hour ritual where ancient myth meets performance art, Balkan Erotic Epic explores the eroticism, spirituality and traditions of Abramović’s homeland through 13 visceral scenes Brought to life by a cast of over 70 performers, dancers, musicians and singers, the experience unfolds across Aviva Studios. Audiences are free to choose their own path – with pop-up encounters punctuating the action, bringing bodies together in dance, song and ritual Watch Fertility Rite , a fevered ritual where bodies writhe against the ground in a desperate call for fertility. Witness Massaging the Breast where women gesticulate over graves to awaken the earth. In Scaring the Gods , women bare themselves to the sky to banish storms. Listen Unafraid to push the boundaries of eroticism and performance art, Balkan Erotic Epic asks its audience a timeless question: What are our bodies truly for?

History, power and empire collide in Button Up! – a major new exhibition from the world-leading artist and activist Ai Weiwei . Internationally renowned artist and activist Ai Weiwei turns his critical gaze to the last 200 years of global history with this major new exhibition. Monumental in scale and ambition, Ai Weiwei: Button Up! is the artist’s most expansive presentation in the North to date.. Ai Weiwei is known around the world for his uncompromising artistic vision and political activism. From a childhood in exile to surviving secret detention in China, his remarkable life and career have led him to global prominence. Using sculpture, installation, film, photography and architecture, his work is unafraid to ask urgent, critical questions.. In Button Up! , the artist turns his lens on two centuries of Chinese and British relations. Taking inspiration from Manchester, a city at the heart of the Industrial Revolution, Button Up! explores how historic systems of trade, empire and exploitation resonate in today’s humanitarian and political crises.. Conceived as a total environment, Ai Weiwei: Button Up! brings together new and existing large-scale works on display in the UK for the first time. The monumental installation features porcelain, cotton, glass, bronze and even buttons and toy bricks. Each material contains a story of human invention and consumption. Together, they paint a picture of globalisation.. Both global and personal, the title Button Up! is a playful poke at the artist’s ongoing battle with censorship. The exhibition also features the world premiere of a new body of work created especially for the vast spaces of the Warehouse – Eight-Nation Alliance Flags made from millions of buttons, as well as a new version of History Of Bombs made entirely from toy bricks.. The new commissions sit alongside large-scale works by the artist which are going on show in the UK for the first time: Law of the Journey (2017), a 47m long inflatable migrant boat containing hundreds of human figures and the artist’s largest artwork to date; Wang Family Ancestral Hall (2015), a Ming dynasty ancestral temple reassembled from 1,500 individual wooden pieces ; and La Commedia Umana (2017-21), a black Murano glass chandelier made up of over 2,000 pieces and weighing nearly 3 tonnes. Also on show is Circle of Animals/Zodiac Heads (2010), a re-envisioning of the twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac.. Button Up! immerses visitors in Ai Weiwei’s fearless interrogation of the forces past and present that drive today’s injustices – while championing art’s enduring power to challenge and inspire.. . . . “I’m not interested in making very big things just for the sake of it. But in Manchester, that wonderful Warehouse space calls for monumental work. Visiting the city for this exhibition – the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution – and reflecting on Britain’s global territorial expansion made me realise I had to explore that history and understand how it connects to the forces driving today’s wars and global crises. The world today is deeply divided, with tragedy all around. Understanding history goes hand in hand with standing up for truth and justice.”. Ai Weiwei. . . Explore. . Ai Weiwei | Dream Space . candidates.evidence_text: for Kids this Summer Holiday Celebrate summer in Manchester with a range of events designed to enchant and entertain the little ones during the school break. The city comes alive with a plethora of family-friendly activities, ensuring that children of all ages have a memorable and joyful experience. candidates.evidence_text: Wednesday 12 May 2027 – Band on the Wall Thursday 13 May 2027 – Southbank Centre Sona Jobarteh is the first professional female kora virtuoso to emerge from any of West Africa’s five Griot dynasties, and a singer, composer and bandleader whose concerts fill some of the world’s finest halls. In 2026 she sold out the Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg, played Munich’s Prinzregententheater and the Schleswig-Holstein Musik Festival, and on October 11 received the Silicon Valley African Film Festival’s 2026 Icon Award for her contributions to African music, scholarship and cultural promotion. On stage, Sona sings and plays the 21-string kora and guitar, joined by Eric Appapoulay, also on guitar, Andi McLean on bass, Yuval Wetzler on drums, Anselmo Neto on percussion and her son, Sidiki Jobarteh, on balafon. The show blends Mandé griot tradition with blues, Afropop and contemporary songwriting. She has also toured with blues legend Taj Mahal. Her concerts have become events wherever she plays. She has performed more than a hundred shows across Europe, Africa, the United States and beyond, in some of the world’s most prestigious theaters and festivals, with sell-outs at London’s Barbican, Cologne’s Philharmonie and the Seine Musicale in Paris, and appearances at the Hollywood Bowl, Symphony Space in New York and WOMAD Australia and New Zealand. Her latest album, Badinyaa Kumoo, was named one of the best albums of its year by Songlines Magazine, and her single “Gambia” has passed 32 million YouTube views. Recent collaborations include a feature on LL Cool J’s album The FORCE, on the song “Black Code Suite”, and a guest appearance on “Se a Vida Pede” from the Brazilian group Gilsons’ latest album. Born in London into a Gambian griot lineage of seven centuries, she began learning the kora at age three with her brother Tunde Jegede and father Sanjally Jobarteh; her cousin was the late Toumani Diabaté. She studied at the Royal College of Music, the Purcell School of Music and SOAS University of London. In 2015 she founded The Gambia Academy, which puts African history and culture at the centre of its curriculum, and she has keynoted forums hosted by the UN and the World Trade Organization. In 2023 Berklee College of Music awarded her an honorary Doctorate in Music alongside Usher and Roberta Flack

candidates.evidence_text: Finish work and unwind with live music from Manchester’s best jazz musicians. Beat the Jams live series showcases the very best of the jazz scene, at short rush hour gigs from 6pm at Band on the Wall. What better way to avoid those endless queues, chaotic traffic and stressful homeward journeys? Clock off and skip the rush-hour traffic while you watch live jazz and make the most of our happy hour deals from 5–7pm: £4.50 pints / 2 for £15 cocktails / £15 bottles of wine + pizzas from £5! The new season kicks off on 24 September with tenor saxophonist Dean Masser and pianist Richard Wetherall, followed by: 7 October – Anna Chandler-King Quartet Leeds based saxophonist and composer Anna joins us again for Beat the Jams, this time with her own band. Anna’s thoughtful and inventive compositions are firm favourites of us at Beat the Jams and her quartet promises to be a unique rush hour busting treat! 16 November – Sam Lightwing Quartet Saxophonist and composer Sam Lightwing brings presents brand new music for his thrilling young quartet, showcasing Sam’s original compositions, which blend classic mainstream jazz grooves with modern flavours of post-pop and latin, all wrapped up in the language of contemporary sax giants such as Chris Potter, Seamus Blake and Joshua Redman. 15 December – Svarc/Devine/Walsh with Richard Iles The band combines deep pocket, fearless interplay and a shared love of exploration. Expect everything from soulful melodies and infectious rhythms to moments of exhilarating collective improvisation, delivered with the chemistry that only world-class musicians can create. Tickets from £13 per show, or £42 for a season ticket

Following their acclaimed album elllegy (RTÉ Radio 1 Best Group), The Olllam has collaborated with GRAMMY-nominated producer Zedd, shared the stage in Belfast with actor Anthony Boyle (Netflix’s House of Guinness), and recently completed a landmark U.S. tour in November 2025. From ancient airs to future soundscapes, The Olllam is not just carrying the tradition forward—they’re reinventing it

Cadno Lounge, Neath . Loungers, the West Country‑based café‑bar group, will open Fosforo Lounge, King Street in Stretford on Saturday 28th November 2026, creating around 30 new jobs for local people.. . Fosforo Lounge will be open all day, every day, serving breakfast, brunch, lunch, dinner and drinks, with dedicated kids’, gluten‑free and vegan menus. . The site on King Street has been transformed by the Loungers design team into a warm, eclectic ‘home from home’ – their signature style. Fosforo translates to matchstick and is a nod to Manchester-based painter LS Lowry’s ‘matchstick men’ style.. . Fosforo Lounge’s all‑day menu will cater for every taste, from hearty comfort food to healthier choices and indulgent treats. Families are a major focus, with games, books, colouring materials, high chairs and baby‑changing facilities available for Little Loungers.. . With community at its heart, Fosforo Lounge will offer a welcoming space for regular meet‑ups, business catch‑ups, book clubs, knitting groups, parent‑and‑baby sessions, creative workshops and more. Local groups looking for a friendly, flexible venue will be encouraged to get in touch.. . Vix Connolly, General Manager, Fosforo Lounge said: “We’re so looking forward to welcoming everyone to Fosforo Lounge on the 28th November. Becoming a genuine part of the community is incredibly important to us, and we can’t wait to meet our neighbours and get involved locally.. . “If you’re looking for a friendly, flexible space for events or group meet‑ups, pop in once we’re open – we’d love to chat and see how we can help.”. . . . . . . candidates.evidence_text: Clint Boon spinning records on Greek Street on a Saturday afternoon, and it won’t cost you a penny. Stopford Park is throwing a free party to launch Bosden, the first of its new apartment buildings, just up from the Town Hall Clint Boon needs very little introduction round these parts. The Inspiral Carpets man was right in the middle of Madchester and he’s still at it, touring and recently publishing his book, The Manchester Chronicles . He’ll be sharing the decks with DJ, presenter and podcaster Matt There’ll be a talk from John Barratt, co-founder of the Stockport Music Story with his wife Rosemary. John founded the record label Facsimile Liaisons which took him to Strawberry Studios, he’s worked with Easterhouse and Syncopation, and also signed The Family Foundation, Ultrac There will be a pop-up from I Knead Pizza, and it’s also the first chance to have a nosey round the show apartment at Bosden with the remaining apartments going on the market the same day. If you’re tempted to have a look round you can register your interest here Make a weekend of it: Foodie Friday is on across the Market Place and Great Underbank the night before, from 6pm

From years spent languishing in post-industrial decline to being crowned one of ‘the coolest neighbourhoods in the world’ in the blink of an eye. What’s the story here? Find out with Jonathan Schofield Tours, with whom you’ll track Ancoats’ changes by strolling its streets, crossing its canals, and taking a look inside one of its most fascinating buildings Starting at Cutting Room Square, your expert tour guide will reveal the layers of history that make Ancoats special, from its place in establishing Manchester’s reputation as ‘Cottonopolis’ to the notorious street gangs, or ‘scuttlers’, who once patrolled and fought here But this winsome stroll is also about the urban regeneration and cultural energy of Ancoats today, which boasts everything from grassroots theatres to Manchester’s only Michelin-starred restaurant

In August, Nothing Gold Can Stay took Robert Frost’s poem about transience as its starting point. Where that show dwelt on things passing, this one is more interested in what lasts The four contributing artists each approach time differently, thinking about how the past and the future shape the way ideas are understood. Anna Clough, a Cumbrian-born artist based at Salford’s Paradise Works, has made walking performances tracing mining landscapes from the Neo Sheffield’s Charlotte Dawson treats everyday objects – souvenirs, collections – as vessels for memory. Olivia England, who graduated from Manchester School of Art alongside Clough, reworks found objects, text and imagery through bookbinding and print, while London-based Elliot Fo Seeing the work from a perspective that isn’t your own is meant to open up conversations about the legacy of ideas, collective memory and what our actions leave behind for people we’ll never meet

candidates.evidence_text: Football Manchester United FC LIVE EVENT ENDED Updated 9 hours ago Man United news: Pochettino 'strikes agreement with board' as exciting stadium announcement made Mauricio Pochettino's reign at Manchester United has begun in the worst possible way and the January transfer Winter is most definitely here and whilst it may be freezing, new United boss Mauricio Pochettino is already feeling the heat.
